stories.headline: Flatbush building collapses beside construction site; deaths confirmed as search continues
stories.summary: A three-story building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, collapsed Wednesday afternoon into an excavated construction site next door, killing at least two people and injuring more than a dozen, city officials said. Later reports Thursday morning put the death toll at three, four or five as rescuers kept searching the rubble. Officials said the cause is under investigation.
stories.why_it_matters: People were killed and injured, children among them, inside a building that housed both apartments and businesses, and the collapse raises questions about how the city protects buildings that sit next to excavation and demolition work.
stories.background: The building stood near the intersection of Flatbush and Bedford Avenues, at the edge of a lot where a one-story building had been torn down for a construction project. It collapsed at around 4 p.m. Wednesday and fell into the neighboring excavation, trapping people inside. It held apartments and a variety of businesses. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the fire commissioner briefed reporters at the scene, and firefighters worked through the night to reach people in the wreckage. NewsNation reported that the neighboring construction site was cited in April and that the company admitted the violation and paid a $10,000 penalty.

facts.text: A three-story building in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighborhood collapsed Wednesday afternoon next to a construction site.
City officials said at least two people were killed.
The building stood at the edge of a lot where a one-story building had been demolished for a construction project, and it fell into the neighboring excavation site.
The collapse happened at around 4 p.m. near the intersection of Flatbush and Bedford Avenues.
Children were among the injured, according to city authorities.
Several people were trapped, and firefighters dug through the rubble to free them; at least one survivor was pulled out.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the fire commissioner gave an update at the scene, and the cause of the collapse is under investigation.
The building held apartments and a variety of businesses.
NewsNation reported that the neighboring site was cited in April and that, according to records, the company admitted the violation and paid a $10,000 penalty.

stories.headline: 17-year-old charged with murder in shooting of Bronx student Javits Frimpong, 15
stories.summary: Police arrested a 17-year-old and charged him with murder in the killing of Javits Frimpong, a 15-year-old who was shot on Oct. 29 while walking to school in the Bronx. Frimpong had moved to New York from Ghana a little over a year earlier. The arrest came about two weeks after the shooting.
stories.why_it_matters: A student was killed on a weekday morning walk to school, and both the victim and the person charged are minors. The case has drawn attention to gun violence among teenagers in the city.
stories.background: Javits Frimpong was a 15-year-old student at DreamYard Preparatory School in the Bronx. He was shot in the stomach near Crotona Park on the morning of Oct. 29 as he walked to school, and he died of his injuries. He had come to New York from Ghana just over a year before. In the days after the shooting, his father told reporters he believed bullying at school may have been connected to the killing. Gothamist reported in June that at least 18 teenagers had been arrested in gun homicides in the city since January.

stories.headline: City Council set to vote on ban on 'surveillance pricing'
stories.summary: The City Council was scheduled to vote Thursday on a bill that would bar businesses from using customers' personal data and algorithms to charge different people different prices for the same goods or services. The New York Times reported that the measure is expected to pass. The bill is sponsored by Council Speaker Julie Menin.
stories.why_it_matters: If the bill becomes law, a store or app in the city could not use what it knows about you, such as your location or shopping history, to set the price you personally are shown.
stories.background: Surveillance pricing means setting an individual customer's price using personal data and an algorithm, so that two people can be charged different amounts for the same item. Speaker Julie Menin and Majority Leader Shaun Abreu introduced Council legislation on dynamic and surveillance pricing in May, and the bill covering surveillance pricing is Introduction 891. The Council held a hearing on the legislation in June. Separately, state lawmakers in Albany voted in June to ban surveillance pricing statewide, a measure Bloomberg Government reported drew industry objections.

facts.text: The City Council was scheduled to vote Thursday on legislation barring businesses from using consumers' personal data and algorithms to charge different prices for the same goods and services.
The New York Times reported that the Council is expected to pass the ban.

The Council held a committee hearing on the dynamic and surveillance pricing legislation in June.

The privacy group EPIC testified in support of the city bill, and the business group Partnership for New York City also submitted testimony.

stories.headline: Council and Mamdani clash in court over $10,000 payments to school paraprofessionals
stories.summary: The New York Post reported that the City Council criticized Mayor Zohran Mamdani in the ongoing court fight over a law giving school paraprofessionals $10,000 payments. The Mamdani administration sued in August to block the law, which the Council passed.
stories.why_it_matters: The outcome decides whether thousands of classroom aides, among the lowest-paid school employees, receive $10,000, and whether the Council can set city workers' pay by law. In today's digest only the right-leaning New York Post covered the latest turn.
stories.background: Paraprofessionals are classroom aides who often work with students with disabilities. The City Council passed a law giving them $10,000 payments, and it took effect on Aug. 19. The Mamdani administration sued the same day; according to The 74, the suit argues the law is unlawful because it bypasses collective bargaining between the city and the union. Outlets describe the money differently: the Post calls it a raise, while The 74 and NY1 call it a bonus.

facts.text: The New York Post reported on Nov. 11 that the City Council criticized the mayor in the legal dispute over the payments.
Paraprofessionals earn as little as $32,000 a year for full-time work, and city public schools have nearly 2,000 vacancies in the job, according to the Post.
The law providing the $10,000 payments took effect on Aug. 19, and the Mamdani administration sued over it that day.
The administration's lawsuit argues the law is unlawful because it bypasses the collective bargaining process, The 74 reported.

stories.headline: THE CITY: New owner of troubled Brooklyn buildings praised by Mamdani has his own violations record
stories.summary: THE CITY reported that Mark Schwartz, the landlord who took over three long-neglected rent-stabilized buildings in Brooklyn in a transfer Mayor Zohran Mamdani celebrated, has what the outlet called a 'dismal' record of violations. The buildings previously belonged to Rubin Dukler, who appeared repeatedly on the city's worst-landlord list.
stories.why_it_matters: The city has presented transfers like this one as a way to rescue tenants from neglected buildings, so the new owner's track record bears on whether conditions actually improve. This is one outlet's own reporting.
stories.background: The Mamdani administration announced in September that three distressed rent-stabilized buildings in Crown Heights, with 88 homes in total, had been sold to a new owner. The previous owner, Rubin Dukler, was a regular on the city's worst-landlord list. The buyer, Mark Schwartz, is also the mayor of Teaneck, New Jersey. Search results describing the deal say the tenants' union reached an agreement with Schwartz on repairs with tenant oversight. The real-estate outlet Bisnow wrote at the time that the city's exact role in the sale was unclear.

stories.headline: Council expected to exempt some severely disabled veterans from property taxes
stories.summary: The City Council was expected to approve legislation Thursday that would exempt some of the city's most severely disabled military veterans from property taxes on their homes. The measure is part of a three-bill veterans package the Council announced Wednesday for Veterans Day.
stories.why_it_matters: Qualifying disabled veterans who own their homes in the city would stop paying property tax on them.
stories.background: New York offers veterans partial property tax exemptions, and a state law now lets local governments choose to grant a full exemption on the primary home of veterans with a 100 percent service-connected disability. Each locality has to vote to adopt it. Port Chester, in Westchester County, was reported in August to be the first municipality in the state to do so. The City Council's bill would apply the idea in New York City.

facts.text: The City Council was expected to vote Thursday on legislation exempting some severely disabled veterans from property taxes on their homes.
The bill is part of a package of three veterans' measures the Council announced Wednesday for Veterans Day.

State lawmakers passed a bill in 2025 allowing a property tax exemption for fully disabled veterans.
